issues.legal_issue: The statutory rules governing intestate succession do not apply when succession opened before those rules came into force.
material_facts: The last male holder of the disputed properties died in 1936–37, before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
A stepmother claimed that she inherited the properties under the Act, although the respondents had obtained a decree recognizing their claim as heirs.
issues.conclusion: Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is not retrospective, and does not apply where the male Hindu died and succession opened before the Act came into force.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 8, the property of a male Hindu dying intestate devolves according to the Act; the words “dying intestate” and “shall devolve,” read in the context of section 6, which expressly concerns a male Hindu who dies after the Act’s commencement, show that section 8 is not retrospective. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.inheritance_claim_under_new_succession_l: A person claims inheritance under a statutory succession law that came into force after the relevant death.
predicates.succession_opened_before_law_commencemen: The person whose estate is claimed died, and succession to the estate opened, before that law came into force.

issues.definition: When an inheritance claim under a new succession law concerns an estate for which succession opened before the law came into force, the new law does not govern.

issues.legal_issue: Possession alone does not make a female Hindu a full owner under section 14(1) when she had no title to the property.
material_facts: The appellant was in possession of part of the properties after her husband died, but the Hindu Women’s Right to Property Act, 1937 had not then come into force in the relevant territory.
When the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force, the appellant had no title to the properties and was in possession without a right to them.
After the respondents sought to execute their decree for possession, the appellant objected, claiming full ownership under section 14(1).
issues.conclusion: The appellant’s possession alone did not attract section 14(1); the provision did not confer title on her because she had no vestige of title and was a trespasser.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, read with its Explanation and subsection (2), enlarges a female Hindu’s existing restricted interest into full ownership; it applies to property in which she has acquired some kind of title, however limited, and does not validate illegal possession or confer title on a trespasser. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.objection_to_execution_of_property_decre: A person objects to execution of a decree requiring delivery of property.
predicates.female_hindu_possesses_property_at_law_c: A female Hindu is in possession of the property when the relevant succession law comes into force.
predicates.no_title_to_property_at_law_commencement: The female Hindu has no legal title or existing interest in the property when that law comes into force.

issues.definition: If a female Hindu in possession of property has no title to it when the law comes into force, her possession alone does not create full ownership, including when she raises that claim in an objection to execution of a property decree.
